articles.title: MK Dons sign goalkeeper Dennis from Bournemouth
articles.summary: MK Dons confirm the signing of goalkeeper Will Dennis from Premier League club Bournemouth for an undisclosed fee.
articles.body:
MK Dons have confirmed the signing of goalkeeper Will Dennis from Premier League club Bournemouth for an undisclosed fee.

Dennis, 26, becomes MK Dons' eighth signing of the summer transfer window, joining the likes of Ryan Barnett , Sam Silvera and Sam Nombe at Stadium MK.

He spent the second half of last season on loan at Leyton Orient, starting the final 14 league games as the O's secured their League One status on the final day of the campaign.

"Will is someone who we have been tracking all summer," head coach Paul Warne told MK Dons' website . "We had to be patient to get our man. However, to improve on our goalkeeping department, we had to make sure we got the acquisition right."

MK Dons have not disclosed the length of Dennis' contract.

articles.title: Printable one-page fantasy football auction value cheat sheets
articles.summary: Every player is available to every team in an auction. The difference is who walks in with a plan and who doesn't.
articles.body:
Fantasy football auction drafts have grown popular because they give every NFL fan equal access to every player, not just whoever a random draft slot happens to land in front of.

Instead of watching a top target get taken by someone else's pick, any manager can buy any name on the board if the budget allows it. That structure rewards preparation and discipline over luck of the draw.

Below is a breakdown of auction strategy by position, along with dedicated approaches for superflex and IDP formats, built around this year's player pool and pricing.

(Note: Cheat sheets can be found at the bottom of the article.)

Patriots quarterback Drake Maye (10) spins a ball on his finger before a game against the Indianapolis Colts at Gillette Stadium.

Enter every auction with tiers, not a strict ranking, so a run on any position doesn't force a reach. Set a max bid on your top targets before bidding opens and hold that number even when the room gets loud. Two builds tend to win. Some call it a stars-and-scrubs build, spending 60-70% of the budget on three or four difference makers, then fill the rest with $1 dart throws.

A balanced build keeps most bids under $30-40 and rosters six or seven dependable starters instead. Either way, never spend more than 70% of the budget on three players, or the back half of the roster gets left to chance.

Nominate players early that you don't want, since it drains rival budgets while your actual targets sit untouched. Late in the draft, flip that and nominate $1 players aggressively to squeeze thin-budget managers out of bench value.

Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts (1) after defeating the Kansas City Chiefs to win Super Bowl LIX at Ceasars Superdome.

Josh Allen tops the position across every format, valued at $30 in standard, $29 in PPR and $28 in half-PPR, but the depth behind him supports waiting. More than a dozen quarterbacks carry legitimate weekly starter upside this year, so paying up early often means passing on a running back or receiver who won't have the same depth of replacement later.

Lamar Jackson and Joe Burrow sit in the next tier around $14-16 across formats, offering a discount on production close to Allen's. If the board gets to Jared Goff or Bo Nix in the $1-4 range, the value gap between the top and the middle has narrowed enough to make waiting the stronger play.

Falcons running back Bijan Robinson (center) carries the ball against San Francisco 49ers safety Ji'Ayir Brown (27) during the third quarter at Levi's Stadium.

Running back still commands the top of every board. Bijan Robinson leads standard at $61 and half-PPR at $59, with Jahmyr Gibbs close behind at $57 and $55. Christian McCaffrey , Jonathan Taylor and Saquon Barkley round out the tier that can anchor a stars and scrubs build.

The middle tiers carry real risk. Backs priced in the $15-25 range, like Kyren Williams or Breece Hall , often come with a clearer path to touches than their price suggests, but committee backfields can sink that value fast. Ashton Jeanty stands out as a value target in that same range, with a cheaper price tag that undercuts veterans with a similar point projection.

Dallas Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb (88) celebrates after a play against the Kansas City Chiefs during the third quarter at AT&T Stadium.

Wide receiver is deep enough this year that patience pays off. Ja'Marr Chase and Puka Nacua anchor the position at $52-59 depending on format, with Jaxon Smith-Njigba , Amon-Ra St. Brown and CeeDee Lamb close behind in the $44-51 range. After that top handful, the price gaps flatten out.

Drake London , George Pickens and Chris Olave sit in the $27-37 range across formats, and the position stays useful well past that point. Malik Nabers , valued around $20-23, is a name to watch for a discount given his target share as a rookie last year, since a shaky quarterback situation is suppressing the price, not his talent.

Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers (89) enters the field before the game against the Cleveland Browns .

Tight end splits into two clear plans this year. Brock Bowers and Trey McBride sit alone at the top, valued between $24-33 depending on format, a real tier above the rest of the position. Paying up secures a weekly scoring edge no other tight end offers. The alternative is fading the position entirely.

Tucker Kraft and Colston Loveland sit in the $16-23 range and offer a credible floor at a fraction of the cost. Depth behind them runs deeper than in past years, so a manager who waits can still land a usable starter for $5 or less late in the draft.

Kickers should be the last dollar spent, not the first. Brandon Aubrey and Ka'imi Fairbairn top the position at $2 across formats, but the gap between a $2 kicker and a $1 kicker rarely shows up in points at the end of the season.

Streaming the position based on weekly matchup beats paying up for name value, since ADP has been a poor predictor of which kicker finishes as a top scorer.

Defense pricing stays flat and low across every format, with the Texans , Seahawks and Rams topping the position at just $2. That flatness reflects how unpredictable defensive scoring is week to week. Spending anything beyond the minimum here takes a dollar away from a roster spot that would matter more.

Treat draft-day defense as a placeholder, then plan to stream the position off the waiver wire once the schedule reveals soft matchups.

Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen signals to the offensive line a play during first half action at Empower Field.

Superflex flips the auction economy since two starting quarterback slots double the position's demand without adding a single passer to the pool.

Josh Allen jumps to $47, with Lamar Jackson and Joe Burrow both climbing to $42, prices that now sit alongside the top running backs and receivers on the board. Budget 35-45% of total spend for quarterback before bidding even opens, since spending like a one-quarterback league here leaves a roster short at the position all year.

Justin Herbert and Jayden Daniels , priced at $36-38, offer a real discount on production close to the top tier. Punting the position outright is rarely worth the points given up over a full season.

Los Angeles Chargers safety Derwin James Jr. (3) reacts against the Las Vegas Raiders during the first half at SoFi Stadium.

IDP scoring flips positional value compared to offense, since linebackers who rack up tackles carry the most weekly point volume. Jordyn Brooks and Jack Campbell top the position at $15-16, with Cedric Gray and Roquan Smith close behind in the $12-14 range.

Defensive linemen and defensive backs price lower across the board, topping out around $9-11 for names like Myles Garrett and Kyle Hamilton . Budget discipline still applies since overspending on the top two or three linebackers leaves little room to fill six total IDP starting spots. Depth at defensive back and defensive line runs deep enough that $1-3 bargains late in the draft can still start every week.

articles.body:
Jeff Brohm is well known for his ability to build an explosive passing game utilizing an assortment of different receivers. The list of NFL receivers who played for Brohm is quite long, and he helped Chris Bell reach his potential last season. This year, Brohm will have a fresh group of pass catchers who have shown the ability to be stars.

The big fish in the transfer portal this winter was Tre Richardson from Vanderbilt. Richardson was a big-play machine in an offense that spread the ball around very well. He was able to showcase his speed as a slot receiver as well as an outside option who could beat coverage down the field. With legit "track speed", Richardson is a guy who needs the ball in his hands on a regular basis. He can change a game with his speed in an instant.

The question that Brohm needs to answer is if he has the ability to scheme Richardson open consistently. That may be with jet sweeps and other plays that get him the ball off the snap. It could also be with quick throws over the middle of the field where Richardson can run away from defenders. I would argue that Brohm needs to incorporate Richardson into the outside passing game. The Cards will be able to push the ball down the field more often this season. Richardson should be an option in that part of the offense.

My hottest take of this entire series is that Lawayne McCoy will have a bigger season than Richardson. The Florida State transfer is the most exciting addition to the team, in my personal opinion. McCoy is a twitchy athlete with good size at 6-1, even though he is a little slight in frame. He was a consistent option for FSU's very poor offense last year, and he showed that he can run the full route tree and showcased a strong ability to make plays after the catch.

Louisville utilized Chris Bell as a do-it-all outside receiver last year and I expect McCoy to be able to carve out a similar role. He doesn't have the size or the long speed that Bell has, but McCoy is quicker and more of a twitchy player who can separate from coverage with his route running. McCoy will have a better offense, a better scheme, and he will likely have a better quarterback this season. I'm expecting big things.

TreyShun Hurry hit the portal for a short while this winter before reversing course to return to the Cards. Hurry will look to take a step up in his role in the offeense after haing a subpar season last year. The 6-2/200 receiver looks much bigger in person but he needs to play to his size this season. He wasn't a reliable deep threat down the sideline last season which has to change.

Louisville lost Kris Hughes to an injury, so depth will be a real question heading into the season. Jackson Voth had a good spring and a strong showing in the spring game while TJ McWilliams has been the main guy who has taken first team reps when starters were out this fall. Elizjah Lewis is the only other player with experience after transferring in from Pace College. One of these guys will have to be a reliable option to make a play or two when needed.

As for the young players, Gavin Waddell has been the standout of the freshmen group. He had the biggest play of the spring game with a 75-yard touchdown on a seam route. He has followed that up with good flashes in fall camp with catches out of the slot and on the outside. I'm not sure if any of the other young receivers will get a lot of snaps this year, but I would be surprised if Waddell isn't on the field early this year.

I truly beleive that McCoy could be a star in this offense. He has all of the traits you want to see in a receiver and he has already showcased them in FSU's game against Florida last year. He can beat coverage down the field, separate on intermediate routes, and he can be used on the outside or in the slot. Brohm has another guy who can do it all, and I expect the strong running game and focus on Richardson to open things up for him.

articles.title: Emiliano Martinez transfer news: Chelsea considering late move for Aston Villa and Argentina goalkeeper
articles.summary: Emiliano Martinez needs to find a new club after Aston Villa signed Zion Suzuki from Parma for nearly £30m; Chelsea's current No 1 goalkeeper Robert Sanchez came under criticism after two errors in Monday's win at Fulham; Martinez was wanted by Juventus but that deal fell through
articles.body:
The Argentina international's representatives have offered Martinez to Chelsea.

Chelsea's current No 1 goalkeeper Robert Sanchez came under criticism after his error in Monday's win at Fulham.

Martinez needs to find a new club after Villa signed Zion Suzuki from Parma for nearly £30m.

Argentina's World Cup-winning goalkeeper was the subject of interest from Juventus but they chose to sign Guglielmo Vicario from Spurs.

WATCH: Chelsea GK Sanchez's two mistakes vs Fulham

Merson: Martinez is one of the best goalkeepers in the world

Martinez is available and he can be hard work sometimes. He comes across like that. But he's one of the best goalkeepers in the world.

And if Chelsea want to get back to being one of the best in the world, you've got to have a top goalkeeper.

Robert Sanchez is usually a good shot stopper. This weekend, or against Arsenal at the Emirates in two weeks' time, he could be mind-blowing. He could make save after save after save and you'll sit there and go: 'Wow.' He could save Chelsea next week.

I don't like picking on goalkeepers because it's a hard job - and you make one mistake for every 50 mistakes the outfield players make with their passing.

But the match against Fulham was another game that he brought the other team back in the game.

At 1-0 you were looking at it and thinking this is going to be three or four. But he lets in a cheap goal and all of a sudden the game has turned on its head really. It looked like Fulham were the team that were going to get the next goal.

I've never known a team ever win anything without a top goalie. I'm sitting there now thinking when was the last time David Raya made a mistake.

The Wolves game in February maybe? But once. In February.

Sanchez makes one mistake a week nearly. And a goal may not come from it, he might kick the ball out for a throw-in.

Against Fulham, Chelsea were dominating, he takes a great catch from a corner and he plays a terrible throw out to Cole Palmer. That happens week in, week out. And the ball could be intercepted, the ball goes back into the box and the opposition score out of nothing.

But I don't think Martinez takes Chelsea towards the title. You look at Arsenal's squad and if you change a player, it hardly weakens the team. Every position is solid.

If you look at Chelsea, they've got a lot of players in each position, but it weakens the team. The name of the game for Chelsea is to make sure when this season finishes, they are playing Champions League football next season. It's as simple as that.

They came 10th last season. And you've got to learn to walk before you can run.

articles.title: Celtic knocked out of Champions League: How will the Hoops respond to collapse in transfer window?
articles.summary: Celtic were on the wrong end of a historic LASK Champions League comeback to deny Martin O'Neill's side a spot in the league-phase draw;Sky Sports News' Anthony Joseph takes us through the implications after Celtic miss out on the Champions League for the second straight season
articles.body:
Four goals ahead with less than an hour still to play across the tie, Celtic somehow found themselves on the wrong end of a 5-4 aggregate defeat to LASK. A place in the league phase was theirs to lose - and they lost it spectacularly, with individual mistakes, questionable decisions and a team that appeared to run out of answers when the pressure mounted.

The fallout will inevitably focus on Martin O'Neill, who took responsibility for the defeat afterwards. But this feels like a much bigger failure than one manager or one night. It raises questions about the squad Celtic have assembled, the decisions made in the transfer market and whether the club were truly prepared for their biggest test of the season.

So, let's break down Celtic's current situation.

Who is to blame - the board, O'Neill, the players?

O'Neill took full responsibility. But the truth is they are all to blame. Should the Celtic players be blowing a four-goal lead with less than an hour to play? No.

Did individual errors and complacency cost them on the night? Yes.

Did O'Neill make the right subs? Probably not - the team was severely weakened with every change and then, similar to Thomas Tuchel's England against Argentina, they were left with no attacking options when the inevitable happened.

But were Celtic fully prepared for this qualifier, compared to last season? They were certainly more prepared.

The signings of Kasper Hogh, Camilo Duran, Mika Baur and Haissem Hassan cost around £32m. They seem to have improved the squad. The starting line-up is stronger. But there were still gaping holes that needed filling.

Celtic knew Arne Engels was likely to leave, but weren't able to replace him in time for LASK. They knew Kieran Tierney needed cover, but they still haven't brought in a back-up left-back. Alistair Johnston's injury was a late blow, but they perhaps should've been ready with a replacement as he was close to leaving before his injury. So, while good signings have been made, they were not fully prepared for this tie.

For a Celtic team to finish a Champions League tie with likes of Dane Murray, Liam Scales, Anthony Ralston and Luke McCowan on the field suggests how threadbare they still are.

Also, it could be argued that postponing their Scottish Premiership match with St Johnstone at the weekend was a mistake, given how dead on their feet the team looked in the second half and in extra time in Austria. Some of them could've done with the extra minutes at the weekend.

Missing out on the Champions League could have huge consequences for Celtic in the last week of the transfer window. Celtic would've been guaranteed another £40m from Europe's premier competition. But they know the reality is much more than that, having made around £75m from their Champions League exploits two seasons ago.

Had they made it there last night, they were expecting to spend in excess of £20m this week on a number of players, including Torino's Gvidas Gineitis and Slovan Liberec's Ermin Mahmic. It remains to be seen whether those deals can still be done, but Gineitis certainly seems unlikely given that he would cost around £10m.

When there's Champions League football on offer, there's no doubt you can operate in a different market. The finances that come with it are huge, but also the lure it has on players is a big draw and sometimes a deciding factor on whether they will join a club in the Scottish league. Even up to yesterday afternoon [Tuesday], it's understood Celtic were being offered some top European talent, via intermediaries, who were seeking to play for a Champions League club this season. That's gone now.

Celtic are in the market for a couple of central midfielders, a goalkeeper, left-back, right-back and possibly even a left winger, before next Thursday's deadline. It's a lot of work to do in a week, with a threadbare team of people doing it but the show must go on to fill the gaps in the squad.

While money is likely to be spent on a midfielder and goalkeeper, some of the other positions may now come from loans. The Celtic hierarchy, recruitment team, O'Neill and Maloney are expected to meet this week to discuss the plan of action for the last week of the window.

How do the club avoid another season of protests and constant negativity?

Despite the glorious ending, last season was a bit of a nightmare for everyone involved in Celtic. No Champions League and poor transfer windows led to mass protests against the board, campaigns to boycott merchandise, a managerial resignation, ultras bans, a managerial sacking and a disjointed team that was carried over the line to a double by O'Neill.

There is only one way to avoid a repeat of last season - and that is for the board to go all out in the transfer market to build a squad that is capable of winning this season's Europa League. Whether the board have the same appetite to do that is another issue. Is it worth them spending big for the Europa League, when financial rewards aren't the same? The fans will certainly think so - and O'Neill might be the man to help give the hierarchy a nudge to help him, not just compete but be a force in the competition.

The fans are also hoping to see a considerable restructure at the club. Celtic still have board members involved in transfer negotiations and football operations. They got rid of their head of football Paul Tisdale in January and still haven't replaced him. There is still no head of recruitment, and they're still a number of first-team analysts short compared with the Brendan Rodgers era.

Celtic's hierarchy had seemed to be patching things up with the fans with their signings and a good domestic start to the season. Yesterday in Linz, chairman Brian Wilson sat and drank with the fans in the afternoon. A lot more patching up is required now.

Will Celtic ever get back to the Champions League?

If Celtic win the league this season, the task of reaching next season's Champions League is even harder. They will enter at the second qualifying round, meaning they will need to negotiate three ties and six matches to get into the league phase of the competition.

This was the last chance for a while that they just had a play-off to win, and it resulted in the sixth consecutive failure they've had in the qualifiers for this competition.

Celtic see themselves as a Champions League club - in stature and size they are. But it could be a while before their team plays in the tournament again.

One direct way into the tournament is by winning the Europa League…
